linkages: Employees matched to employers using the Firm-Integrated Database for Labor Market Research, which links workers to firms in the employment spell of week 48 of each year only; for workers with multiple employers in that spell the primary employer (by hours worked) is used.
IDA individual records matched to Lonstatistikken (LON) hours records and to Firmstat / Foreign Trade Statistics firm records.

sample.universe: Full-time employees aged 15-65 in Denmark, 2003-11, with data available from all sources (IDA, LON, Firmstat), employed in private firms.
sample.unit_of_observation: worker-year for the labor-supply analysis (worker observed in 2008 and 2011 for the tax-reform regressions); firm-year for the hours-constraints analysis
selection_rules: Full-time employees only, defined (per the official definition in place) as those working more than an average of 26 weekly hours over a 1-year period (approximately 90% of the sample).
Only firms with available data on the number of hours worked for at least 95% of the workforce in a year.
Workers linked to their primary employer (selected on hours worked) in the week-48 employment spell; annualized hours and earnings for spells shorter than a year.
For the tax-reform regressions: workers present in both 2008 and 2011 and at the same firm in 2008 and 2011.

High-income workers = middle or top tax bracket in 2008, excluding the 'residual group' (2008 top-bracket workers predicted to be in the bottom bracket in 2011); low-income workers = tax exempt or bottom bracket in 2008.
sample.n_observations: 787,683 worker-year observations in the final sample (table 1, col. 5)

construction_notes: Hours constraints sigma_jt (eq. [1]) = standard deviation, across skill groups within a firm-year, of the mean annual hours worked in each skill group; measured at annual frequency; LOWER sigma = STRICTER constraints.

Skill groups = deciles of the distribution of estimated worker skill s_ijt = X'_ijt beta-hat + alpha-hat_i from an Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis firm-worker fixed-effect model of hourly wages (appendix sec. B.1); an alternative definition from education x occupation cells gives similar results.
Table 3 reports STANDARDIZED coefficients; each cell is a different regression of sigma_jt on one firm characteristic and a constant.

Marginal tax rates are not observed; they are simulated by extending the Danish tax simulator of Kleven and Schultz (2014) to 2006-11, as the increase in tax liability from a DKK 100 increase in labor income holding other income components constant.
Mechanical tax-rate changes (the instruments) apply the post-reform schedule to base-year income adjusted for inflation.
Tax-reform regressions relate 3-year log changes (2008 to 2011 in the baseline) and weight observations by labor income.
Table 4 and table 6 use TOTAL hours (regular and overtime) of high-income workers; table 5 uses REGULAR hours for both low- and high-income workers.
Earnings, value added, capital and sales are deflated with the consumer price index, base year 2000 (DKK 8 = USD 1 in 2000).
O*NET contact/teamwork/communication scores range 0-100; the median score across coworkers in a firm-year is used; this analysis is restricted to 2003-9 when ISCO-88 is consistently available.

claims.statement: The firm-level measure of hours constraints (the standard deviation of mean hours across skill groups) varies substantially across firms, with a 90th-to-10th percentile ratio of approximately 100, which the authors read as evidence that the measure does not merely reflect sorting of workers with similar hours preferences into firms.

register_source.value: Firm Statistics Register (Firmstat) and Firm-Integrated Database for Labor Market Research, matched to Lonstatistikken (LON) hours

definition.value: The unit of observation is the firm-year; the figure plots the distribution of the hours-constraints measure across firm-years, weighted by firm size.

outcome.label: Hours constraints: standard deviation of mean hours (regular and overtime) worked across skill groups within a firm and year

register_source.value: Lonstatistikken (LON): annual hours of regular and overtime work

definition.value: sigma_jt in equation (1): the standard deviation, across the skill groups present in firm j in year t, of the group-mean annual hours h-tilde_sjt. Skill groups are deciles of the distribution of estimated worker skill from an Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis wage model. Lower values indicate stricter constraints.

units.value: ratio of the 90th to the 10th percentile of the distribution of the hours-constraints measure across firms

magnitude.interpretation: The paper reads the wide dispersion as evidence that the measure captures firm-level constraints rather than perfect sorting of workers on hours preferences, since under pervasive sorting the measure would be small or close to zero in all firms.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-firm variation in the measured dispersion of hours across skill groups; no exogenous variation is used.

key_assumptions.assumption: A low value of the standard deviation of mean hours across skill groups indicates stricter hours constraints, because workers in different skill groups have heterogeneous desired hours.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Labor force survey evidence that the least skilled workers desire to work approximately 15% fewer hours (five weekly hours) than the most skilled workers (table C.5).

key_assumptions.assumption: The measure reflects firm-level constraints rather than sorting of workers with similar hours preferences across firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The 90/10 ratio of the distribution of the measure is approximately 100 (fig. 1); desired hours differ across skill groups (tables C.5, C.6); tax-induced changes in high-income marginal tax rates do not significantly affect the measure (table C.10, col. 8).

threats_discussed: The measure could capture individual preferences rather than firm constraints if workers with similar desired hours sort perfectly, or pervasively, across firms.
robustness_checks: Alternative measures of hours constraints: SD of hours across high-income workers, across all workers irrespective of skill, and including part-timers (appendix secs. D.2-D.4).
Alternative definition of skill groups from education x occupation cells (appendix sec. D.1).

evidence.annotation: FIG. 1.-Distribution of hours constraints. This figure presents the distribution of hours constraints measured as the standard deviation of mean hours (regular and overtime) worked across skill groups within a firm and year. We define skill groups as deciles of the distribution of alpha-hat_i + X'_ijt beta-hat estimated from the Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis model (for details, see sec. B.1 of the appendix). For each firm and year, we plot the value of the standard deviation of hours across skill groups weighted by firm size. Each bin in the histogram is 10 hours long. To comply with Danish micro data usage regulation, we do not show the top 5% of the distribution because it would result in a number of observations below the allowed limit in some bins.
